prize_parts.citation: For the theoretical prediction and experimental discovery of the quantum spin Hall effect and topological insulators

statement.case_for: B057 is a clear, independently verified discovery of a new class of quantum matter, in which protected edge and surface states follow from band topology rather than from symmetry breaking. It has the full arc the committee should look for. Kane and Mele made a sharp theoretical proposal (the Z2 classification and the quantum spin Hall idea), and Molenkamp's HgTe/CdTe transport measurement showed the effect in the lab. That result was then reproduced and extended by ARPES, transport and many material families over about two decades. From where I sit as an electronic-structure theorist, the physics is also quantitatively predictable: band inversion and spin-orbit coupling, computed from first principles, reproduce what experiment sees. That link between calculation and measured spectra is what makes me trust a result. It is also a reminder that quantum mechanics keeps surprising us. The field is mature and has produced real downstream work in spintronics and in quantum-device concepts, and recognition is timely and arguably overdue.
statement.case_against: The strongest objection is attribution. Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang made the HgTe prediction that Molenkamp's experiment tested, and the three-dimensional topological insulator work (Fu, Kane and Mele; Moore and Balents; Hasan) is also outside the three-name credit. The three-person limit makes any boundary arguable. A second objection is that the 2016 prize for topological phases and phase transitions might make a topology prize look incremental, so the committee would need to say clearly what this adds: topology in band structure of real materials, rather than in model systems and phase transitions. I also read the opening ballots as showing that B057 has broad but shallow support (seven ranked, only two in the top three), while B027 has broader first-tier backing, so I should not mistake my own first place for committee consensus.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks the optical lattice clock first as a clean atomic-physics case where theory and experiment agree at about 1e-18, and she notes that the 2005 and 2012 prizes could be read either for or against another clock prize. She ranks B057 sixth, and asks whether the credited list omits arguably decisive people.
responses.response: I take the lattice clock seriously: I placed it fifth and I agree that the two-name credit (Katori and Ye) is cleaner than ours, and that maturity and timing are excellent. My reservation is one of novelty. The clock is an extraordinary refinement of precision that earlier prizes (2005 combs, 2012 ion control) opened, whereas B057 introduced a new organising principle. I accept her point that our credit list omits people, and I agree that this is the real weakness in B057. I do not think it is fatal, since the 2005 theoretical proposal and the 2007 experiment are unambiguous milestones. If the committee finds the BHZ question unresolved, I would move the clock to the top rather than force an unsettled B057.

responses.point: Kroll argues the lattice clock is the clearest case on the list of a technique that changed what can be measured, that Katori and Ye form a clean pair, and that it is timely given the planned redefinition of the second. He puts it first.
responses.response: I agree with most of this, including the clean credit and the independent confirmation across many national labs, which is the kind of robustness I ask about first. Where I differ is on weighing. A tool that changes what we can measure is a strong prize case, but I place somewhat more weight on a discovery that changes what we think matter can be. I also note that the redefinition of the second has not yet happened, so timing is a plus but not decisive, and the clock will not be harmed by waiting a cycle. I would therefore call B027 my first alternative rather than my choice, and I would not object strongly if the committee preferred it.

responses.point: Olsson ranks topological insulators fourth, calls it a major conceptual advance with verified edge transport, but flags that the omission of Bernevig, Hughes, Zhang and the 3D work, together with overlap with the 2016 prize, could weigh against timing.
responses.response: I think she has stated the two central worries correctly. On the 2016 overlap, I would answer that the 2016 citation concerns topological phase transitions and topological phases of matter in model systems (the quantum Hall effect, Haldane's chain and Kosterlitz-Thouless physics), while B057 concerns time-reversal-invariant topological band insulators found in real materials, so it is a distinct discovery and not a repeat. On credit, I would like the committee to examine the sequence carefully: Kane and Mele 2005, then Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang 2006, then Konig, Molenkamp and colleagues 2007. I concede that an honest citation would need to be worded around the theoretical proposal and the first experimental observation, and that I am working from memory on priority details.

responses.point: Johansson ranks circuit QED first and trapped-ion logic second, and defers partly to condensed-matter colleagues on B057, while noting that Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang, and the 3D topological insulator work, make for a real credit dispute. He also flags that his own work in circuit QED may bias him and that the 2025 prize recognised superconducting circuits.
responses.response: I appreciate his frankness about proximity and I try to apply the same standard to myself. His credit objection to B057 is fair and I do not want to wave it away. I would stress that Kane and Mele's Z2 formulation was what made the effect a general classification of band insulators, and Molenkamp's measurement is the decisive confirmation, so the trio is a defensible core even if the full historical record is wider. On B036, I share his view that the field is mature, but the 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum tunnelling in superconducting circuits makes a close successor harder to justify this year, and I cannot rank it above the clock or topological work on that account.

uncertainties: Whether the committee can settle credit for the HgTe prediction (Bernevig, Hughes, Zhang) and for the 3D topological insulators within a three-person limit, given that the supplied names exclude them.
Whether the 2016 prize on topological phases is judged to overlap enough with B057 to count against it.
Whether the committee would rather reward the lattice clock (B027), which has wider first-tier support and a cleaner two-name credit, in this cycle.
My recollection of priority and dates is from memory and has not been verified against the nomination record.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile. I have no known personal or institutional tie to Kane, Mele, Molenkamp, Katori, Ye, Bloch, Greiner or Zoller. As a theorist of electronic structure and magnetism I am professionally close to the topological-materials field and to Hubbard-model physics, which I will treat as a possible bias toward B057 and B006 and not as a recusal matter.
